items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: Twice as far doesn't mean half the gravity — it means a QUARTER
items.claim: Gravity, Coulomb force, light intensity, radio signal strength all follow inverse-square laws. Move twice as far away and you don't halve the strength — you quarter it. The geometry of 3D space, not physics, drives this.

options.text: The same total 'flux' (energy, field lines, or whatever flows outward) spreads over a sphere whose surface area grows as r^2. Intensity per unit area falls as 1/r^2 — geometric, not physical

items.reveal:
Newton's gravity: F = G * m1 * m2 / r^2.
Coulomb's law: F = k * q1 * q2 / r^2.
Light intensity: I = power / (4 * pi * r^2).
Gravitational and electromagnetic potential energy: U ∝ 1/r.

The common thread: in 3D space, the surface area of a sphere of radius r is 4 * pi * r^2. Any quantity radiating outward (energy, electric field, gravitational influence) spreads over this growing area. Intensity per unit area scales as 1/r^2.

If we lived in 2D, the analogous laws would be 1/r (intensity spreads over a circumference of 2 * pi * r). In 4D, it would be 1/r^3. The dimensionality of space is encoded in the exponent.

In fact, modern physics tests for 'higher-dimensional' theories by looking for deviations from 1/r^2 at very short ranges. So far, none seen down to ~10^(-5) metres.

Applications:
- Move twice as far from a fire: get 1/4 the warmth.
- Move three times as far from a noise source: hear 1/9 the intensity (sound pressure decreases as 1/r in spherical waves, intensity ∝ pressure squared = 1/r^2).
- Stars further away appear dimmer by 1/r^2 — leveraged for cosmic distance measurement (standard candles).
- Cell phone signal degradation as you walk away from a tower follows 1/r^n where n depends on environment (line-of-sight ~2, urban ~3-4 due to obstacles).

Kepler's third law (T^2 ∝ a^3) and Newton's gravity were unified because the 1/r^2 force law is precisely what makes elliptical orbits work — Newton's biggest mathematical victory.
items.why: The 1/r^2 pattern looks like a coincidence of physics. It's actually the geometry of 3D space showing up everywhere. The exponent IS the dimensionality.

items.title: A 99% accurate medical test for a rare disease usually gives a false positive
items.claim: A test for a rare disease is 99% accurate (1% false positive rate, 1% false negative rate). The disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have the disease? Roughly 1%, not 99%.

options.text: Base rate matters. Out of 10,000 random people: ~1 truly has the disease (and tests positive); ~100 don't have it but test positive anyway (1% of 9999). Total positives ~101, true positives 1. So P(disease given positive) ≈ 1/101 ≈ 1%
False positives are impossible for accurate tests

items.reveal:
Bayes's theorem: P(disease | positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) / P(positive).

P(positive | disease) = 0.99 (test sensitivity).
P(disease) = 0.0001 (base rate — the prevalence).
P(positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) + P(positive | no disease) * P(no disease) = 0.99 * 0.0001 + 0.01 * 0.9999 ≈ 0.0001 + 0.01 = 0.0101.
P(disease | positive) = 0.99 * 0.0001 / 0.0101 ≈ 0.0098 = 0.98%.

The 'accuracy' of the test is misleading when the disease is rare. The vast majority of positives are FALSE positives, drawn from the much larger pool of healthy people.

Key insight: rare conditions produce rare true positives. Even excellent tests produce overwhelming numbers of false positives in screening contexts.

Real-world implications:
- Mass screening for rare cancers, HIV, etc., requires careful interpretation of positives.
- Drug tests at low real-prevalence give many false accusations.
- Airport security: very low base rate of terrorists; almost all positives are false alarms.
- Mammograms in the 40-49 age group: famous case of low base rate leading to controversy over screening recommendations.

Professionals routinely misinterpret. Gigerenzer's studies show many doctors get this wrong on similar problems. Communicating in 'natural frequencies' (1 in 10,000) rather than probabilities (0.0001) helps people reason correctly.
items.why: Test accuracy seems to translate directly to confidence in results. Bayes's theorem forces a different interpretation: when the condition is rare, even sensitive tests produce mostly false positives. Whole branches of medicine and public policy depend on getting this right.
